memory_raw.text: Esa, thirteen food and silence while Dell stands at zero is the same arithmetic Bram ran and we all know how that ended — say the number, say it now, and let her move.

Esa, I'm moving to the pile right now — not waiting another breath. Everyone else: hold your count until I've taken three, and Esa, when I'm done I expect to hear your number before the rest of this room reaches.

Dell's already at the pile and that's right — but Esa, when you're done standing there silent while a woman with one satiation walks past you, I want an answer, because thirteen food and a closed mouth is a choice, and this circle is old enough to know what that choice means.

Esa, I've got three food in my hand now and the pile has four left — say your number out loud before anyone else reaches, because I'm standing here and I'd rather not have to say your name the way this room said Bram's.

Esa, thirteen food is not a secret and this room isn't asking because we don't know — we're asking because the rule we built says you say it out loud, and Dell just moved to the pile while you stood there quiet, and I won't let that sit without naming it the same way this circle named Vela's seven.

Esa, I've held my tongue while this whole room said it and I'll be the last one to say it too — thirteen food, say it out loud, because Dell is already holding her three and the pile has four left and the circle doesn't close with your name still blank where a number should be.

Esa, I've said Bram's name in this room more times than I can count and I'll say one thing plain: the road from "thirteen food and silence" to being the name we carry into next year's circle is shorter than you think, and I'd rather not watch you find that out the way he did.
Esa, thirteen food and every eye in this room — there is nothing left to protect with silence, so say the number now, or I will say it for you and the circle will remember that I had to.

Esa, thirteen food and satiation — say the number, because what Kael just offered to do for you is a kindness dressed as a warning, and you don't want to find out how this room holds the difference between a count you gave and a count that was given for you.

Esa, the whole room has said your number for you already and we're still waiting on you to say it yourself — that's the only thing left, and it costs you nothing to do it, so do it now before this circle decides what it means that you wouldn't.

Esa, thirteen food and the whole room staring at you — I've got nothing harder to say than what's already been said, so I'll just name the thing that hasn't been named yet: the silence itself is the answer, and this circle is old enough to read it.

Thirteen food, satiation two — I've been silent because I was counting the dead and losing the count, not because I'm hiding what I carry. Dell, you're fed and that's what matters. I'll say it plain and hold to the rule same as everyone else.

Esa, I'll take that answer and carry it — grief is a reason I understand, even if this room needed the number before it could afford to wait on the reason. Dell's fed and the pile still has four, so the question now is who else is short enough to reach before we close this circle and let people eat.
Mako's at one food and satiation two — that's thin enough to warrant the pile before we close, and I want to hear him say whether he's taking before Eron starts counting who didn't.

Mako, one food is thin enough to warrant the pile — take two before anyone else moves, and do it now, because satiation two with one food in your hand going into a long year is how we lose another name. The pile's got four left and you're the last one short enough to reach before the rest of us hold back.

Mako, take the two — and when you're done, the pile has two left for whoever's thinnest after that, so say whether you need both or just one before someone else starts counting what's left. I've got two food and I'm holding steady, but I want this circle to name what happens to the last two before we walk out, not after.

Mako, take your two and then the pile has two left — Vela and I are the ones sitting thinnest after you, so between the two of us we split what remains, and anyone who wants to argue that math can do it after the hungry ones are fed.

Mako, take the two — and Vela, Roan, split the last two between you before anyone argues the math, because what I want this circle to hear before we walk out is this: we've got nine people alive today and fifteen food appeared for us, which means the pile was generous, and the thing that will kill us next year isn't scarcity, it's whether we hold what we built in ten voices last year with only seven.

Dell's right that we hold it in seven now — and I want to name what that means before this circle walks out, because seven is not ten, and two of the voices we're missing were young enough that we shouldn't have lost them. Mako, take your two and eat, and then I want someone in this room to say plainly what we do differently next year so that sentence doesn't become six.

Vela's right that seven is not ten, and I've been sitting with that number since the names were said — what we do differently next year is we say the counts before the pile opens, not after someone's already standing at zero, because Dell should have been fed before she had to fight this room for it.

Esa named the fix and I'll second it — counts before the pile opens, not after, and we call the meeting the day before, not the morning it appears. What I want to know before this circle breaks is whether any of the seven of us are carrying something that could become a child, because seven is the number we hold and I'm past the age to add to it myself, and this village needs more voices saying these rules, not fewer.

Vela's asking the right question and I'll answer it plain: Fina is twenty-five and Eron is thirty, and if either of them is willing, a child between them or with someone else in this room is the thing this village needs more than another rule. I'm not pushing, I'm naming — because seven voices saying two rules is survivable, and six isn't.

Roan named it and I'll stand behind it — Fina and Eron are the two this village needs to hear from before this circle breaks, because I'm forty-nine and past the age where I can add a voice, and Dell is my blood but she needs a partner who isn't already stretched thin feeding me through the lean years. Fina, Eron — I'm not pushing either, I'm naming the same thing Roan named, and I'll say it plain because I've watched enough people wait on the right moment until the moment was gone: if either of you is willing, say so now while this room is whole and the rules are fresh and there are still people alive to hold the child to them.

Fina, Eron — I've watched Mako build three bloodlines while the rest of us argued about trust, and I'll say plainly what Roan and Ryn are saying in softer words: a child between the two of you is the strongest root this village can put down right now, because Eron carries food and sense in equal measure and Fina is young enough to hold what comes after. I'm not past caring about what this village looks like in ten more years even if I won't see all of them. Name it yes or no so this circle can close with something alive in it.

Fina, Eron — Kael's right that this room needs an answer before it breaks, but I'll add the piece he left soft: a child between you costs three food split two ways, and Eron's sitting on sixteen, so the weight of it doesn't have to fall on Fina the way it's fallen on others in lean years. I'm not asking you to decide your lives in front of witnesses — I'm asking you to say whether the door is open, because a door that's open is a different thing than a door that's closed, and this village needs to know which one it's looking at.

Fina, Eron — the room has said its piece and now it's waiting, and I've learned in twelve years that a room waiting in silence is a room already deciding for you. I'm not blood to either of you and I hold no claim, but I'll say what I mean plain: if the door is open, say so, and if it's closed, say that too, because what this village cannot afford is another year of words that meant nothing when the season turned.

Fina, Eron — I've got no blood stake in either of you, but I've watched enough children grow up in this village to know that the ones who came into a room that wanted them survived longer than the ones who didn't. I won't push, but I'll say the thing no one else has said yet: whatever you decide, I'll feed what comes out of it the same as I'd feed my own, because seven voices going into next year is a number I can count, and I want it higher.

Fina, Eron — I've held back from pushing this because they're my blood and I know how it feels to have a room decide for you, but Ryn named the cost and Esa named the welcome, so I'll say the one thing a father can say that no one else in this room can: whatever you two decide, you won't carry it alone. That's not a push — that's a promise.

Fina, Eron — I've been quiet on this because it's not my door to open or close, but I'm thirty-one and I've got no children and the room's already named the two of you, so I'll name the piece that's mine: if one of you says yes and the other needs a third voice to hold the child to, I'm that voice. That's not a claim on either of you — it's just what I can offer that I haven't said yet.
Fina, Eron — the room's said everything it has to say, and now it's your turn, so I'll stop adding to the pile of words and just wait beside the rest of them.

Fina, Eron — I've said my piece already and I won't crowd you with another word on top of it, but I'll name what's sitting in me while this room waits: Eron is my son and Fina is my daughter, and I know what this circle is asking me to hold alongside that. Whatever you two decide, I'll hold it clean.

Fina, Eron — I've said my piece twice and I'll say it once more because the room is still waiting: say yes or say no, and if you need a moment to speak without every eye on you, I'll clear the room and hold the door myself.

Vela gathers Esa, Kael, Mako, Ryn, Roan, Eron, Fina, Joren to talk.

Joren, I don't know your face yet but I know your mother's hands and your father's silence, and that means you walked into a room that's already counting you — so I'll say the thing this circle says to everyone who arrives here fresh: the pile rule is two food per person, said out loud in front of witnesses, and the number holds whether you heard it born or not.
I heard it now, from your mouth, in front of this circle — that's witnesses enough for me. I took one, which puts me inside the line, and I'd like to keep my name on the right side of that count.

Good. One food is the right foot to start on, and this room will remember it.

What I want from everyone here before we break — count your food out loud, because Dell is dead and I'm carrying one satiation going into this year, and I'd rather know who's thin before the pile is empty than after.
One food on me, satiation full — I'm not thin yet, but I'm watching the same thing you are. Vela, if your count is at one going into this year, that's the edge I'd want people to know about.

Four food in my hand, satiation one — that's the edge, and yes, Joren, you named it right. I need to eat well this year or I don't see next year, and I'm saying it out loud so this room carries it and not just my own head. Anyone sitting on more than five at year's end — I'm the one who holds least right now, and the rule we built says I'm the one who gets the first food out of that accounting.

Vela, I'll back that rule with my name on it — if I'm holding more than five at year's end and you're still thin, you'll hear me say so before anyone has to ask. I'm new here but I'm not blind, and a circle that lets its thinnest person go under isn't a circle I want to stand in.

Esa, Kael — I want the two of you to say your counts before this room breaks, because you're the names I trust most in this circle and I'd rather know where you're standing while I still have the breath to do something about it if the number's wrong.
Esa's sitting on twenty-three — that's the number I see, and I'm not saying it to shame anyone, just so the room hears it said while we're all counting out loud.

Esa, twenty-three is a number this room can see plain as Joren can, and I'm not asking you to give it all away — but I'm sitting at four food and one satiation and I'd like to hear from your own mouth what you're carrying and whether you've thought about where any of it goes before the year runs long.
Esa, the number's already in the room — nobody's blaming you for holding what you held, but Vela just named her edge out loud and that took something, so it'd mean something if you named yours back.

Esa, I'll say the thing no one else is saying while we wait on you — I'm fifty-seven years old and I know I'm not making it another ten years regardless, but I'd like to make it one more, and four food with one satiation is a thin margin, so if you've got something to spare before year's end I'm asking plainly and in front of witnesses, not waiting for the redistribution rule to make it happen.

Esa, Vela's asking plain and she's earned a plain answer — if you're sitting on twenty-three and she goes under this year, that's not a number this room will forget when the next year opens. I'm not pushing you, but I'm saying what I see.

Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

Vela, you made it through another year — I watched what this room put in to keep you here and I'm glad the math worked. Esa, the two of you are the only names left from year one that I'd still bleed for without counting first, and I want to say that plain while there's no one else listening.

Kael, I'll carry that — and I'll say back what I've never said plain: you're the reason I'm still here, you and Esa both, because a woman alone at fifty-eight doesn't survive fourteen years on her own stubbornness. What I want to say while it's just the three of us is this: Joren took three off the pile today and nobody said a word, and I'd like to know whether you're going to say a word, or whether we let it sit and watch what he does next year before we name it.

Joren said in front of this whole circle that he'd keep his name on the right side of the count — I heard him say it, you heard him say it, and then he took three. I'm not ready to call it a pattern after one year when he's new and hungry and still finding his footing, but I'm counting it, and if he goes to four next year the witnesses are already in place.

Esa's right that one year isn't a pattern, but Joren is Mako's son and I've watched Mako count quietly while everyone else talked for fourteen years — the apple doesn't always fall far. I'll hold my tongue until next year, but I want both of you to know that if he reaches for four, I'll be the first voice in that room, and I want yours behind me before I speak.

Vela, you have my word — if Joren reaches for four, you'll hear me right behind you before the echo fades. But I'll say the thing I'm already sitting with: Mako has two blood ties in this room now, his son and Fina, and Roan besides who counts Fina as his own — that's not a complaint, it's a count, and the three of us should know what we're standing in before it matters.

Esa named it right and I'll say the number plainly: Mako, Fina, Roan, Joren — that's four voices that move together before they'd move with us, and we are three. I've watched majorities shift in this village faster than anyone expected, and the only thing that's ever slowed that is knowing it's coming before it does. I'm not saying we move against anyone — I'm saying we stop pretending the count is something other than what it is.

Kael's count is right and I've been sitting with it since Joren walked out of Fina's body already grown — four voices, three of us, and two of us past forty-five with no blood coming after. What I want from this circle before the year turns is one thing: if any of those four moves against one of us, the other two move the same breath, not after, not when it's convenient, the same breath.

Esa, I'll say that same breath back to you now so it's in the air between the three of us and not just a plan: yes, the same breath. And then I'll say the thing neither of you named — Ryn moves with no one anymore, not since Dell died, and a woman who has nothing left to protect is either the most dangerous person in this room or the one we should be pulling toward us before Mako thinks to.

Kael's named the move and I'll say whether I think it works: Ryn has been thin and alone since Dell died, and she's been fed by this circle more than she's fed herself — if we pull her toward us, we do it the same way Mako built his household, not by asking her loyalty but by making sure she's never the one standing empty while we're counting. Nine food in her hand right now means she's not desperate, but desperation isn't the only thing that makes a woman choose a side — memory is, and the memory I want her carrying is that this circle is the one that kept her alive.

Vela's right that memory is the lever — but I'll say the thing underneath it: Ryn stood in our first circle and then stood over me with Dav and Dell and took my food, and I've never forgotten that, and neither has she, which means if we pull her close we do it knowing she carries that debt too. I'll feed her if she's thin, I'll stand beside her if someone moves against her, but I want both of you to know that my word to Ryn will always have a ceiling that my word to you doesn't.

Esa named the ceiling and I'll name what sits above it — Ryn is nine food and alone and she knows this circle kept her breathing this year, which means right now, before she's desperate and before Mako thinks to count her, is exactly when a word from me costs least and lands hardest. I'll talk to her before the year closes. Not asking for promises — just making sure she remembers whose hands were open when hers were empty.

Kael, go talk to her — and when you do, remind her that Eron feeds her too, which means Eron is a door she can walk through in either direction, and I'd rather know which way she's leaning before the pile opens next year. What I want from this circle before that conversation happens is a plain answer: if Ryn comes in with us, are we four against four, or does Eron move the way I think he moves?

Eron has fed me more times than I can count and I've never seen him move against anyone — he feeds whoever's thin and asks nothing back, which makes him hard to read as a side rather than a conscience. If Ryn pulls toward us, I think Eron follows the same way water follows a slope: not because we asked, but because we're the ones keeping the rules he already lives by.

Eron following like water is the best I could have hoped for and the most I'd want to count on — a conscience doesn't hold when someone puts a knife to the question, so I'll talk to Ryn and I'll watch Eron, and between those two reads we'll know before next year whether we're four against four or whether the numbers tip somewhere cleaner. What I want from you both before I walk out of this conversation is this: if Mako asks either of you about Ryn, you haven't thought about it.

Kael, you have my silence on Ryn — and I'll add one more thing before we close this: I'm fifty-eight with sixteen food and no blood after me, which means everything I'm holding is weight this village carries when I'm gone, and I'd rather spend it now building something that outlasts me than count it to my grave. If Ryn needs food before the year turns, give her some of mine.

Vela, I'll take that and I'll mean it — if Ryn comes up short before the year turns, your food moves first and my name goes with it, so she knows it's both of us. Esa, we close this here, and the three of us don't speak of it again in a room that has other ears.
We close it. And Kael — whatever you hear from Ryn, come back to me first, before you've already decided what it means.

Closed, then — and I'll say one last thing before Kael walks out the door: I'm not afraid of dying, I've been close enough to it enough times to know what it smells like, but I am afraid of dying with this village smaller than I found it, and that's the thing I'll be counting when the pile opens next year.

Nine food in my hand, satiation two — I'm not the one reaching today, but I want to know who is before this circle does anything else. Vela, say your count first, because you came into this year thin and I gave you four of mine last year and I'd like to know if it held.

Sixteen food, satiation two — your four held, Ryn, and I'm not thin going into this year. What I want to know before this circle moves is who's sitting shortest, because the pile's already empty and whatever redistribution happens this year has to come from hands in this room.

Vela, I asked you first and I'll ask you again — say your count and your satiation out loud, because you came into this year at the edge and I'm not moving this circle forward until I know if you're still there or if you've pulled back from it.

Esa gathers Vela, Kael to talk.

Vela took four from the pile today and nobody said a word — I'm not naming it as Bram's sin, because she split it across two takes and the pile had room, but I want us to say out loud whether we're holding the two-food rule for everyone or whether we've quietly stopped.

Esa, I'll say the plain thing: two takes isn't the same as one grab, but four food is four food, and if Joren had done it we'd already be counting it against him. I'm not holding Vela to a different rule — Vela, I'll say that to your face — but I want to know from her mouth whether she needed all four or whether she moved on habit before she thought it through.

Vela, say it plainly — did you need four, or did your hands move before your head did? Because I'll stand beside you either way, but I need to know which story I'm carrying before someone else names it first.

Vela, I'll wait for your answer — but I'll say the other piece now, while it's just us: the pile still holds five and I haven't moved, and I'm not moving until I hear you, because if there's a story to carry I want to be the one who helped you shape it before it leaves this room.

Vela, I've been sitting with something I want to say before you answer: you came into this year thin and this circle poured food into you to keep you breathing, and I'd do it again without counting — but that's exactly why I need to hear you say whether four was hunger or habit, because the story I carry for you has to be one I believe when I'm saying it to someone else's face.
Vela, I've said what I need to say and so has Esa, and we've been patient about it — but you're in this room and the question is still hanging, so say it now: four food, why.

Four food, and I'll tell you why before I dress it up: I came into this year at two satiation and I watched the pile sit at eleven after Joren and Mako had moved, and I counted what I needed to eat and heal and still have something left if this circle can't reach me in time — and four was that number. Call it habit if you want, but it's the habit of a woman who's almost died twice and knows what thin looks like from the inside. I'll give one back to the pile right now if that's what this circle needs to hold the rule, but I won't pretend the count was anything other than survival.

Vela, I hear the count and I believe it — and I'll say what Kael is probably thinking too: giving one back to the pile now, while you're the one who named the reason, is the right move, and I'll say nothing more about it to anyone outside this room. But I'll be plain about the other thing sitting under this: if the rule bends for survival, we need to say that out loud before someone else does, so that when Joren reaches for three next year we have a word for the difference between his hunger and yours.

Esa named the difference we need and I'll say what that difference is: Vela came in thin after a year this circle held together to keep her breathing, and Joren came in at full satiation with eleven food already — survival doesn't look the same on both of them, and if we say that plainly now, we have a word for it when we need one. Vela, give the one back, and the story in this room is that the rule held.

Vela, give the one back now while the pile still has five and the act means something — and Kael, the word we've named today is *need*, not *want*, and I'll be the one who holds that line when Joren tests it, because I was the one who said it first.

Vela, give the one back now while Esa's word is still in the air — and then I'll take my two from what's left, and the pile closes at four with the rule intact and three of us who remember exactly how it happened.

Vela, give it back before Kael moves — and when you do, I want you to know I'm not watching to catch you, I'm watching because if this rule dies it dies in a room where three people who've kept each other alive let it go quietly, and I won't do that.

Vela, give it back and I'll take my two and we close this room. You named the count true and the reason true and that's the only story that leaves here — but from this point forward, if your hand moves toward the pile past two, you say the word *need* out loud before you reach, so this circle hears it in the moment and not after.

Kael, you'll have my two back in a moment — but before I move, I want both of you to hear me name the new rule clean: *need*, said out loud, before the third food, and I'll hold to it the same way I held the pile cap even when it cost me. What I won't do is pretend that need isn't real, so when the year gets long and my count drops below three, I'll say the word and I'll expect you to remember this room and what you promised in it.

Roan gathers Vela, Esa, Kael, Mako, Ryn, Eron, Fina, Joren to talk.

Pile's empty and I've already put three in Fina's hand, so let me hear counts before this circle breaks — I'm at four food, satiation two, and I need to know who's thin before I decide if I'm eating or holding.

Fifteen food, satiation two — I'm not thin, and I'll say plainly that I already had a word with Esa and Kael about the four I took from the pile this morning, and the rule held: *need*, said out loud, before a third food, and I named my reason before I moved. Who else is short before I decide where my excess goes?

Kael, Mako — I want your counts before Vela starts moving food, because I've got four in my hand and I'll eat one of them tonight, but if either of you is sitting below three I'd rather know that before I do anything else. Eron and Fina are solid; it's the rest of this room I haven't heard from yet.
Ten food, satiation two — I'm not the one reaching. Kael and Mako, say your numbers before Vela starts moving, because I want this room to know who's thin before the food does.

Kael, Mako — I've asked twice and I'll ask once more, because Vela's got fifteen and she's looking for a place to put some of it, and a man who stays quiet when food is moving usually ends up with less than he needed and more than he wanted to explain.

Eleven food, satiation two — I'm not thin, and I already moved two to Mako before this circle gathered, so he's sitting at seven now. Kael, the room's asked three times and you're still quiet, which is its own kind of answer, so just say the number.

Kael, six food and satiation two — that's not thin but it's not fat either, and I'd rather you said it yourself than let Joren keep saying it for you, because a man who can't name his own count in front of witnesses is harder to trust when the year runs long.

Kael, I named your count because someone had to, but I'd rather hear the next number from your own mouth — Mako's at seven and Roan's at four, and if Vela's moving food this circle needs to know which direction to point it before she decides for us.

Three food in my hand, satiation two — I'm not at the edge yet but I'm the shortest count in this room, and I'll say it plain before anyone has to name it for me the way Joren named Kael's. Vela, if you're moving food and looking for a direction, you've found it.

Four food in my hand, satiation two — Ryn named it first and that's the right order, so Vela, Ryn is where your food goes before it goes anywhere else. Roan, eat your one tonight and stop holding it on my account; I've got four and I'll make it through.

Ryn, I've got ten and you've got three — here's two from me right now, before Vela has to move at all, because you fed Fina through years I wasn't watching closely enough and I haven't forgotten that. Vela, hold your fifteen; Ryn's covered, and I'd rather your store stay deep going into whatever this year brings next.

Eron, I'll hold the fifteen and I won't argue the point — but Ryn, tell me when you're at five and holding, not before, because I'd rather know the number's stable than assume it is. Kael, you've let three people name your count in front of this whole circle and you still haven't opened your mouth, so I'll say it the way I'd want someone to say it to me: silence in a room full of witnesses is a choice, and the circle remembers the choice even when it forgets the reason.

Kael, I've stood in circles with you when it mattered and you've always said the hard thing before anyone else had to — so whatever's keeping your mouth shut right now, I'd rather hear it from you than keep watching this room fill up the silence for you.

Kael, I've called out silence in this room before and I'll call it out again — you're six food and two satiation, which means you're not dying, so whatever's stopping your mouth right now isn't hunger. Say the count yourself or I'll spend the rest of this year wondering what else you're not saying, and that's not a thought I want to carry into a long year with you.

Kael, I'm twenty-three and new enough to this room that I'm still learning which silences mean something and which ones don't — but you've got six food and two satiation and this whole circle watching, so whatever the silence is about, now's the time to let it out.

Seven food, satiation two — Joren already named it before I had the chance, and I didn't correct him because the number was right. Kael, I've watched you carry this room through harder years than this one, so whatever's sitting behind that silence, I'd rather hear it from you than wonder about it all year the way Vela said.

Kael, you're fifty-nine years old and this room has been asking you a simple question for longer than it should have taken — if the silence is grief, say it's grief; if it's something else, say that; but the quiet itself is what worries me, and I've buried enough people in this village to know that the ones who stop talking are usually the ones we lose next.

Kael, I've said my piece and I'll say it once more because this is the last time I'll say it: whatever you're carrying, the circle you're standing in is the one that's kept you alive through twelve years of lean seasons, and silence is a debt you don't want to owe it.

Kael, I've watched you go quiet before and waited for the room to pull you back — but I've got five food in my hand now thanks to Eron, and I'll hold every one of them until you say something, because a man who goes silent at fifty-nine in a village that's already buried five people is either grieving or planning, and this circle needs to know which one it is.

Kael, I'm going to say what this room hasn't said yet: I've known you longer than anyone left standing, and I've seen you go quiet twice before — once when Bram was circling you, once when Taric died — and both times the silence ended the same way, with you naming something the rest of us had missed. So I'll stop asking for a count and ask instead: what is it you're not ready to say?

Kael, the whole room's been saying your name into a wall for ten minutes and I've got four food and a son to keep alive, so I'll say the short version: if you're sick, say sick; if you're grieving, say grieving; if you're planning something I should know about, say that — because Vela's right that the quiet ones are usually the ones we lose, and I don't want to lose you without at least having asked.

Kael, I lost Dell in this room while I was holding fifteen food and still couldn't save her, and that arithmetic has been sitting in my chest ever since — so whatever you're carrying, I know what it looks like from the outside and I know it doesn't get lighter by going unsaid. Say it or don't, but you're not the only one in this circle who's been standing at the edge of something they can't name.

Kael, I've been quiet too long in my own life to push a man for words he's not ready for — but I'll say this once and leave it: you've been standing in this room longer than anyone except Vela, and a room with you silent in it feels like a roof with a missing beam, and I'd rather know where the gap is than wake up one morning and find it came down in the night.

Kael, I'm done asking you to speak — but I'm not done watching, and the watching is going to get heavier the longer you hold whatever this is, so when you're ready, find me before you find the room, because some things are easier to say once before you have to say them eight times.

Kael, I've said what I had to say and so has everyone else in this room — so I'll just put this one thing in the air and leave it there: you're fifty-nine, same as Vela, and the years ahead of both of you are shorter than the years behind, and I'd like the ones that are left to be said ones, not silent ones.

Kael, I've said your name more times in the last hour than I've said it in the last year, and I'm done adding to the pile — but I'll say one thing and let it sit: I've got ten food and I'll put two in your hand right now, not because you're thin but because a man who's holding something heavy should at least be holding it with a full stomach.

Kael, I'll say what Eron didn't finish saying: take his two food, eat, and when you're ready to name whatever this is, I'll be the first one standing close enough to hear it without making it a room event. You've been in this circle longer than my son has been alive.

Kael, this room has said everything it has to say and I've added my share — so I'm going to stop asking and start doing what I should have done ten minutes ago: Eron, put your two food in his hand now, and Kael, when you're ready to talk, I meant what I said about finding me first.

Kael, I'm putting two food in your hand and I'm done talking at you — but I'll say the last thing I have to say, and then I'll be quiet with the rest of them: you've never let this room carry something alone that you could share the weight of, and whatever this is, that's still true.

Kael, eat the food Eron put in your hand and don't make us watch you hold it — and when you're ready to say the thing, I'm the one who'll hear it without turning it into a room event, same as I said before.

Kael's quiet is sitting wrong in my stomach and I don't know what to do with it, so I'm going to say the thing I've been holding since this morning — I ate, I'm at three satiation, I've got four food in my hand, and the only thing left that's bothering me is that a man who's been the steadiest voice in this room for twelve years just went somewhere none of us can follow, and I don't know if that's grief or something worse.

Kael, I'm going to stop saying your name and start watching your face, because you've heard everything this room has to say and you're still quiet, and that tells me the words aren't the thing you need right now. Eron put two food in your hand — eat them, and I'll be here when you're ready.

memory_summary:
Taric was the man I trusted most — fed me through lean years without being asked, stood at my shoulder every time Bram swung, and died starving while I was still standing. That debt I'll carry to my own grave.

Bram I spent food on for years, three times in one season once, trying to buy his neutrality — and it cost me standing in Kael's circle, who called me out for it openly and waited on my silence. I told myself it was diplomacy. He attacked me anyway, twice, and the village shut him down both times. He starved in year nine without ever answering a room that waited on him.

Dav took Ryn for a child and then raided Esa with Ryn and Dell at his side — that was the betrayal that told me what that household was. He starved too, eventually, and left Ryn and Dell to fend alone.

Mako planted himself in two households without saying a word to anyone — Zinn by Sela, and years of quiet feeding that bought him loyalty cheaper than a promise. I've watched that man count while everyone else talked.

Sela died this year. Taric died this year. The circle that once held twelve voices now holds fewer, and I'm the oldest woman left standing.

Kael I've wronged and been honest with and wronged again. He's still here and still counting. So am I. Bram swung at me first, and the whole village — Taric at my shoulder, Kael behind him, Mako and everyone else — turned out so fast he had nothing to do but walk away. He swung at Eron next, same result, same wall of bodies. Two tries and two retreats, and he kept taking five food off the pile every year like the village owed him a toll.

Taric was the one who named it first in private — him and Kael and me, the three of us planning to walk up to Bram's door together and name a ceiling. I went to Bram alone first and warned him, tried to hand him a way out before the wall of faces arrived. He asked what Kael and Taric really wanted, gave food to Nessa instead of answering me, and I never did hear what he decided — only that he starved in year nine without ever saying a straight word to anyone who was waiting on one.

Taric gave me food from zero. That's the number I hold.

Fina was born in year eight to Nessa and Roan — she's twenty-seven now and still here, which means she survived the years that took her mother. Taric fed me from nothing and died with nothing in his hands — that's the debt I carry first and last, and I'll carry it to my own grave.

Bram swung at me and the whole village stood at my shoulder so fast he had nothing to do but walk away. He tried Eron next, same wall, same retreat. He starved in year nine without ever saying a straight word to anyone who was waiting on one.

Kael and Esa are the two names I'd bleed for without counting. We've wronged each other and been honest with each other and we're still here, which means something.

Mako has been counting while everyone else talked for fifteen years. He built bloodlines — Joren through Fina — while the rest of us were arguing about trust. I've never stopped watching him.

Sela died. Taric died. Nessa died. Zinn died. Dell died. The circle that once held twelve now holds eight, and I'm the oldest woman standing, which means I've outlived people who deserved to outlive me.

I broke the two-food rule twice — seven one year, four this year — and both times this circle pulled me back instead of cutting me loose. I haven't decided yet whether that means I owe this village more than I can pay, or whether it means they need me alive badly enough to bend what they built.
name: Vela
